detail: Clear, first-principles framing (the healthy wall actively keeps platelets off). The simplified note is honest.
suggestion: Optional: open with the problem being solved, e.g. 'Blood must not clot inside healthy vessels, so the lining actively holds platelets off.'

detail: Lists 'thrombin' (not introduced until the cascade module) and implies ADP and TXA2 come from the broken wall. Really they come from other activated platelets (and thrombin from the cascade). Only collagen is actually 'exposed' at the break.
suggestion: Rewrite: 'At a break, platelets touch exposed collagen. Once a few platelets switch on, they release ADP and thromboxane A2 (and the clotting cascade makes thrombin), which switch on more.' Add a glossary entry for thrombin or mark it as a forward reference to Module 2.

detail: Good push-pull framing an EMT can hold onto (one brake, one gas). Needs 'aggregation' glossed (see glossary flags).

The second source (sp-txa2) passage is garbled ('While prostaglandin counterbalances ... prostacyclin (PGI2) has various physiological and pathological situations...') and does not cleanly support the claim. The sp-hemostasis passage alone supports it.
suggestion: Drop the sp-txa2 passage or replace it with a clean sentence.

detail: Accurate and practical. EMTs will connect it to why a cut vessel bleeds less after a moment.

The sp-hemostasis passage ('Within about 30 minutes of damage... vascular spasm ensues') is about when spasm begins, not how long it lasts. It does not support the duration claim, and read literally it conflicts with 'spasm is the first, immediate response' in c-et-1. The OpenStax passage alone supports the claim.
suggestion: Remove the sp-hemostasis passage from c-et-2 (and from c-plt-4, where it is used the same way).

detail: The claim is correct but has no 'so what'. On the street this matters: a wound that stopped bleeding can start again as spasm relaxes, as the patient warms up, or as BP rises.
suggestion: Add one line: 'Spasm is temporary, so a wound that looks controlled can re-bleed; keep reassessing.'

detail: Good: defines 'subendothelial' inline ('the collagen underneath it').
Accurate and well pitched. Its card_front 'What does vWF bridge between at a wound?' is awkward.
suggestion: Card front: 'At a wound, what two things does vWF connect?'

detail: 'Weibel-Palade bodies' and 'alpha granules' are both new jargon in one sentence, and the fact has low value for an EMT-B. Weibel-Palade bodies have no glossary entry.
suggestion: Simplify to 'vWF is stored ready-made inside the vessel lining cells and inside platelets, so it can be released fast at an injury.' Put the Weibel-Palade name in a 'simplified' note, or gloss it.

detail: Introduces 'factor VIII' with no definition. An EMT-B with no biochemistry does not know what a numbered clotting factor is, and Module 1 has not introduced the cascade yet.
suggestion: Add a glossary entry for 'clotting factor / factor VIII' (e.g. 'a clotting protein; missing in hemophilia A') and link it with [[factor VIII]].

detail: 'High-shear' is physics jargon. The parenthetical helps, but 'shear' is still not defined. The fact is also more detailed than an EMT-B needs.
suggestion: Write 'fast-moving blood that drags along the vessel wall (high shear)' and add a glossary entry for 'shear'. Consider marking this claim as enrichment rather than core.

detail: Clear. Depends on 'receptor' and 'glycoprotein' being glossed.
suggestion: Link [[receptor]].

detail: Accurate. It is a rare disease, but useful as a clean contrast with Glanzmann (adhesion vs aggregation).

detail: Good. 'Positive feedback' should be known from EMT A&P (e.g. childbirth), but a glossary link would be cheap.

detail: 'Granule' is never defined. 'Small molecules vs proteins' is a biochemistry distinction this learner does not have. The text says 'storage sacs', which helps, but there is no tappable entry.
suggestion: Add a glossary entry for 'granule' (a storage packet inside the platelet that it dumps out when activated). Keep the 'small chemical signals vs large proteins' wording plain.

suggestion: Add glossary entries for fibrin and coagulation cascade/secondary hemostasis. Optionally add: 'This is why sustained direct pressure matters: the early plug is fragile.'

detail: Correct and street-relevant (the best EMS hook in the module). 'Purpura' and 'mucosal' are not EMT-B vocabulary, and petechiae is borderline. There is no contrast with the factor-problem pattern (deep and joint bleeds), which is what makes the pattern useful in assessment.
suggestion: Gloss petechiae, purpura and mucosal. Add: '(By contrast, clotting-factor problems like hemophilia tend to cause deep bleeding into joints and muscles. Module 2.)'

detail: Accurate. '/µL' is a unit an EMT-B may not read fluently.
suggestion: Gloss µL (microliter) or write 'per microliter'. Note that lab reports often show this as '150' (×10³/µL).

detail: Accurate. The two thresholds (10k vs 20k) are honestly hedged with 'about'.
Strong misconception claim. Minor point: in vWD the platelets themselves are normal and the anchor (vWF) is missing.
suggestion: Consider: 'yet platelets can't adhere properly because their anchor, vWF, is low or faulty.'

detail: Accurate, well pitched, and street-relevant (a history of nosebleeds, heavy periods and bruising).

Accurate and clear. EMT-Bs give aspirin for suspected ACS, and this module never links the mechanism to that use. A one-line bridge would anchor the whole module for this learner (no full drug entry needed).
suggestion: Optional: 'This is why aspirin is given for a suspected heart attack: it weakens platelet plugs forming on a ruptured plaque in a coronary artery.'

detail: Accurate and well reasoned.

'CYP2C19' is undefined jargon. For an EMT-B the useful takeaway is 'the liver has to activate it, and some people's livers don't do this well', not the enzyme name. The card front makes the enzyme name the point being tested.

detail: 'Lasts 7–10 days' and 'recovers often within about 5 days' in one sentence reads as a contradiction to a novice.
suggestion: Explain: 'Each blocked platelet stays blocked for its 7–10 day life, but because new platelets keep arriving, overall function is often mostly back within about 5 days.'

The title gives the answers away (lists GPIb, P2Y12, GPIIb/IIIa). P2Y12 is not 'used at a step' of the four steps the way GPIb (adhesion) and GPIIb/IIIa (aggregation) are; it is an activation signal receptor. 'At each step' therefore does not map cleanly onto g01's four steps.
suggestion: Retitle: 'Match each platelet receptor to its step (adhesion, activation, aggregation)'.

detail: EMT-B pharm touches 'receptor' loosely (beta receptors), but it is never defined for this learner, and it is the core idea of the module. Appears in c-vwf-1, c-gpib-1, c-adp-1, c-p2y12-1, c-clop-1, c-gp2-1, c-fgn-1, c-gpib-2, c-gp2-3, q03, q04, q05, q11, q14, q15, q22, q23, q26, q27, goal m1-g02, cards.
suggestion: 'A receptor is a specific docking spot on a cell's surface. When the right molecule fits it, the cell responds, the way a key fits a lock.'

detail: Appears in node names and aliases (GPIb 'glycoprotein Ib', GPIIb/IIIa 'glycoprotein IIb/IIIa'), in accepted answers (q03, q04), and in c-endo-1 sources and simplified ('glycoproteins such as thrombomodulin').
suggestion: 'A protein with sugar chains attached. The "GP" in GPIb and GPIIb/IIIa stands for glycoprotein.'

detail: Appears in c-vwf-2, c-dg-1, c-ag-1, c-adp-1, c-gpib-1 sources, goal m1-g03, q06, q07, q10#3, q27#1, cards, node names 'Dense granules' and 'Alpha granules'.
suggestion: 'A small storage packet inside a platelet. When the platelet activates, it dumps the packets' contents outside to signal other platelets.'

detail: A technical step name an EMT-B will mix up with aggregation. Appears in c-plt-4, c-gpib-1, c-gp2-2, c-vwf-3, goals g01 and g02, q01, q10, q14, q26, q27.
suggestion: 'Adhesion = platelets sticking to the damaged vessel wall (via vWF). Compare aggregation = platelets sticking to each other.'

detail: Appears in c-pgi2-1, c-plt-4, c-adp-1, c-p2y12-1, c-clop-1, c-gp2-1, c-gp2-2, c-gp2-3, c-asa-1, q01, q04, q05, q09, q14, q15, q22, q26, q27.
suggestion: 'Aggregation = platelets clumping onto each other, bridged by fibrinogen, to build the plug.'

detail: 'Activated' and 'activation' are used throughout (c-endo-1, c-endo-2, c-gpib-1, c-plt-3, c-plt-5, c-txa2-1, c-gp2-1, q01, q14, q27) without saying what changes in an activated platelet.
suggestion: 'An activated platelet has been switched on: it changes shape, releases its granules, and turns on GPIIb/IIIa so it can clump.'

detail: The module's own title term. Appears in c-plt-4, c-plug-1, c-plug-2, c-pc-3, goal g01, q01, q17#2, q16#2, q20#3, q22#1, q24#2.
suggestion: 'Hemostasis = stopping bleeding. Primary = the platelet plug (minutes). Secondary = the clotting cascade that reinforces it with fibrin.'

detail: Appears in c-plug-1, c-fgn-1 context, q02#1, q11#1, q14, q16, q17#1, q20#1, q12#1, q18#2, q24#1, q26#2, card-c-plug-1. Not introduced until Module 2.
suggestion: 'Fibrin is the tough protein mesh, made from fibrinogen by the clotting cascade, that reinforces the platelet plug into a durable clot.'

detail: Appears in c-plug-1, card-c-plug-1, q16#1, q16#2, q17#2, and the c-plt-4 source passage.
suggestion: 'A chain of clotting proteins in the blood, each switching on the next, that ends by making fibrin. Covered in Module 2.'

detail: Appears in c-endo-2 (and its card) and q06#3 (distractor). Not explained in Module 1.
suggestion: 'Thrombin is the clotting enzyme that turns fibrinogen into fibrin and strongly activates platelets. Covered in Module 2.'

detail: Appears in c-vwf-3, c-vwd-2, q09#2 (distractor), q11#1, q25#3, cards. An EMT-B knows hemophilia but not numbered factors.
suggestion: 'Clotting factors are blood proteins numbered I–XIII that run the clotting cascade. Factor VIII is the one missing in hemophilia A.'

detail: Appears in c-vwd-2, card-c-vwd-2, q25#3 explanation. Many EMT-Bs know 'hemophilia' but not the A/B distinction. Low priority.
suggestion: 'An inherited lack of factor VIII; causes deep bleeding into joints and muscles.'

detail: Appears in c-cox-1, card-c-cox-1, q13#1, q13#2.
suggestion: 'A fatty acid pulled from the cell membrane; COX-1 turns it into the chemicals that become thromboxane A2.' Or drop the name from learner-facing text.

detail: Appears in c-vwf-2, card-c-vwf-2, q06#1 (distractor).
suggestion: 'Storage packets inside vessel-lining cells that hold vWF, ready to release at an injury.'

detail: Appears in c-vwf-4, card-c-vwf-4, q11#2.
suggestion: 'Shear is the dragging force of fast-moving blood along the vessel wall; it is highest in arteries and small vessels.'

detail: Appears in c-plug-2, card-c-plug-2, q24#2. Many EMT-Bs learn it (meningitis, strangulation), but not all programs teach it. Given its street value, gloss it.
suggestion: 'Pinpoint red-purple dots on the skin from tiny bleeds; they don't fade when pressed.'

detail: Appears in c-plug-2, card-c-plug-2, q24#2 explanation. Not EMT-B vocabulary.
suggestion: 'Larger purple patches from bleeding under the skin, bigger than petechiae but smaller than a typical bruise.'

detail: Appears in c-plug-2, card-c-plug-2, q24#2. EMT-Bs know 'mucous membranes' but 'mucosal bleeding' as a pattern needs anchoring.
suggestion: 'Bleeding from moist linings: nose, gums, mouth, gut, heavy periods.'

detail: Defined only inside c-pc-1 and as an alias of the platelet-count node. Used in q19#3, q24#2 and c-pc-2 sources. It is a tappable word learners will see on med lists.
suggestion: 'A low platelet count, below 150,000 per microliter.' Link [[thrombocytopenia]].

detail: Appears in c-pc-1, c-pc-2, q19, q24. EMT-Bs rarely read lab units, and real lab sheets show '150' (×10³/µL), which will confuse.
suggestion: 'µL = microliter, a millionth of a liter. Labs often write the platelet count as 150–450 (meaning thousands per µL).'

detail: Appears in c-clop-2, card-c-clop-2, g-pro-1 why_here. Also CYP3A4 in simplified notes and sources.
suggestion: 'A liver enzyme that activates clopidogrel. Some people inherit a weak version, so clopidogrel works poorly for them.'

detail: Appears in c-plt-5, c-txa2-1, cards, q12#1. Often taught in EMT A&P (childbirth), so this is low priority.
suggestion: 'A loop where a response causes more of itself, like activated platelets releasing signals that activate more platelets.'

detail: This is the key concept for g10 and g11. Appears in c-asa-1, c-asa-2, c-clop-1, c-pras-1, c-tica-1, q20, q22, q23#2.
suggestion: 'Irreversible: the drug locks onto its target permanently, so the effect lasts until the body makes new targets (new platelets). Reversible: the drug lets go, so the effect fades as the drug leaves the blood.'

detail: Usually glossed inline as 'vessel lining', but it appears bare in many places: c-endo-1, c-col-1, c-vwf-2, q08, q09#3, q10#2, goal g04, cards. EMT-B curricula don't reliably teach the word.
suggestion: 'The single layer of cells lining the inside of every blood vessel.'

detail: Glossed inline in c-col-1, but used bare in the node name 'Subendothelial collagen' and in q10#3.
suggestion: 'Beneath the vessel lining.' Or make it an alias of an endothelium entry.

detail: No EMS note in the module is wrong. Missing in ways that matter on the street: (1) c-asa-1 never connects aspirin's COX-1 mechanism to why EMT-Bs give aspirin for suspected ACS, the single biggest relevance hook for this learner. (2) c-plug-1 and c-et-2 do not connect to direct pressure or re-bleeding (spasm relaxes in ~30 min; the plug is fragile until fibrin reinforces it). (3) c-plug-2 lacks the contrast with factor-type bleeding (joints and deep muscle), which is what makes the pattern useful in assessment. (4) q20#2 frames 'must stop aspirin before surgery' as a rule; it should not read as advice EMTs give patients.
suggestion: Add one-line street bridges to c-asa-1, c-plug-1/c-et-2 and c-plug-2, and reword q20#2 as noted. Full drug EMS entries remain deferred to Module 6.
